title: Northbridge intro — streamed chat gen + retry patterns
summary: AE+SE walkthrough of Redwood Hosted API for streaming chat and text generation. Covered streaming behavior, parameters (temperature, max_tokens, stop), retry/backoff patterns, idempotency, and console observability. Customer asked about latency vs cost tradeoffs, data residency, SOC2, VPC/private options. Agreed next steps: send pricing, SOC2 kit, schedule security deep dive and SE-led benchmark run.
action_items: Ava - send list pricing + sample committed-use options - 2026-05-20
Liam - share sandbox runbook and a short demo replay clip showing streaming partials - 2026-05-21
Priya - run a small latency benchmark with Northbridge sample payloads (SE-assisted) - 2026-05-25
next_steps: Schedule security deep dive with Jenny and Rafael (30-45m)
Provision a sandbox project and share credentials and a short tutorial video
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-18
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Northbridge), Maya (Northbridge PM), Rafael (Northbridge CTO), Jenny (Northbridge Security)

[00:00] Ava: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we've got about 45 minutes, we'll run through a quick hosted demo of streamed chat generation and then leave time for q and a. uh my name's ava with redwood.
[00:18] Ethan: hey, thanks. excited, we want to understand how streaming partials work and how retries won't kill our UX.
[00:27] Liam: cool, i'll drive the console tour and demo. quick context check—what's your current stack for messages? are you on a kinesis queue + node backend or something else?
[00:38] Maya: right now it's kafka -> node api gateway -> our message service. latency budget is ~200ms p50 for typing indicator but we tolerate 600ms p95 for generation. cost is a big driver.
[00:52] Rafael: also, we operate in us-east but have european customers so data residency matters. we may move to a private deployment later.
[01:03] Liam: got it. we'll show the hosted api first — it's the fastest onramp. note: in the console you can toggle streaming and watch partial tokens arrive as events.

[02:10] (screen share starts)
[02:22] Liam: ok sharing console now. on the left is model catalog, we pick a 16k context open model for this demo. you'll see 'stream' checkbox which turns on chunked responses. important: streaming sends incremental deltas, so your UI should render them as they arrive — that's what gives that streaming typing feel.
[02:45] Maya: are those deltas guaranteed in order? sometimes in our infra we see out of order events.
[02:53] Priya: generally yes, the service preserves order per request but if you re-try or fallback to a different model variant you'll see a restart token. there's a request-id header to reconcile fragments.
[03:12] Ethan: and how does retrying work — we panic when a request drops mid-stream.
[03:19] Liam: two patterns — client-side naive retry (which can cause duplicates) and server-side resume. with redwood you can opt for idempotency keys. include the same idempotency key with retried requests and the server reconciles. if streaming was partially delivered, the server can return a resume offset so the client can request the remaining tokens.
[03:46] Maya: resume offset? that's interesting, do you mean you keep a KV-cache of token offsets?
[03:52] Liam: yeah that's the rough idea — the runtime keeps a small session state for a configurable TTL so a resume is possible within a short window. it's not infinite but it's effective for transient network blips. (note: sometimes the transcript shows "kv cache" as "k v cash" but it's the same.)

[04:30] Ava: quick pause—on pricing tradeoffs, lower latency often needs higher tier models or dedicated pools which cost more; batching and prefix caching can lower unit costs but increase tail latency for some flows.
[04:50] Rafael: so what if we need strict p95 < 300ms and low cost?
[04:56] Liam: you can run a hybrid—dedicated capacity for high volume endpoints and hosted for lower volume. also configure small batch windows and aggressive KV caching for repeated prefixes. we'll share quantization profiles that reduce GPU time for many workloads.

[06:00] (demo: POST /v1/chat/completions)
[06:12] Liam: here's a raw call: we send messages array, set stream:true, set temperature 0.2, max_tokens 120. you'll see server-sent-events come back with delta chunks. here's an example payload.
[06:36] Ethan: what about cancellations — our app cancels after 3s when user hits stop.
[06:43] Priya: cancellation is a normal pattern; we surface a cancel endpoint and we try to stop GPU work ASAP. cancellations still count for billing as partial tokens may have been generated, we show partial token counts in the console.
[07:00] Maya: any best practice for stop sequences?
[07:06] Liam: use stop tokens and max_tokens plus early termination heuristic in client. also send a streaming 'end' event to gracefully finalize UI.

[08:20] Ava: security question time — do you have SOC2 and what about SSO?
[08:27] Jenny: yeah we'll need SOC2 type II, SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and KMS integration or bring-you-own-key.
[08:36] Ava: we are SOC2 compliant; we'll send the kit. we support SAML/SSO and RBAC through the console. for private deployments we offer KMS/HSM integration and VPC peering.
[08:52] Jenny: good to know. also on data retention — we can't allow training on customer data.
[08:58] Priya: Redwood's hosted policy is opt-out of model training for enterprise customers; we also have options to disable telemetry. we'll share the security whitepaper showing retention controls.

[09:35] (transcript note: occasional mis-attribution — Speaker 2 labelled as Lara in the ASR)

[10:05] Liam: back to retries — typical backoff we recommend exponential backoff with jitter. we have SDK helpers that implement idempotency and resume semantics. if you need at-least-once semantics, it's straightforward but your client should dedupe by request id.
[10:34] Ethan: can you show us how the console surfaces failed requests and the token breakdown?
[10:40] (screen)
[10:45] Liam: here, per-request traces include latency histogram, per-token timing, and cost estimation. the console also ties tokens back to API keys so you can see team-level cost attribution.
[11:03] Maya: is there an alerting integration? slack/pager?
[11:07] Ava: yes, console hooks to webhook alerts and prometheus exporters for custom dashboards.

[12:00] (demo: retry scenario)
[12:12] Liam: i'm going to simulate a transient error. you'll see the client retry with the same idempotency key and the server returns a resume offset.
[12:30] (sound of keyboard)
[12:45] Ethan: ok i see the stream resume, UI continues, no double renders. that's promising.

[13:15] Rafael: what about throughput? we have spikes around product launches, need autoscaling.
[13:22] Priya: dedicated pools scale horizontally with pre-warmed nodes and burst capacity. autoscale configs can be rule-based or usage-based. hosted service also has burst lanes but we can discuss reserved capacity for predictable throughput.

[14:30] Maya: earlier you mentioned quantization—does that affect output quality?
[14:37] Liam: some quantization modes (e.g. 4-bit) have small quality regressions depending on model/precision. Redwood Optimize (sometimes mis-transcribed as 'Redwood Opti-mize') includes evaluation recommendations — we can run evals on your prompt set to find the lowest precision with acceptable quality.
[15:05] Ethan: will you run that evaluation on our prompts?
[15:09] Priya: yes, that's a standard part of the POC we propose. we'll need a representative prompt set and good/failure examples.

[16:00] Jenny: about data residency — can hosted ensure eu-only processing for eu customers?
[16:07] Ava: yes, we route requests by region and can pin data to eu zones. for stronger guarantees we offer Private (VPC) or an on-prem bundle.

[17:10] Ethan: are logs encrypted at rest?
[17:14] Ava: yes — logs and artifacts encrypted, and we integrate with customer KMS in private deployments.

[18:30] Maya: what's the typical timeline to go from pilot to prod? we have a roadmap that needs production in q3.
[18:38] Liam: pilot typically 2-4 weeks for sandbox validation, then 4-8 weeks for production-ready integration depending on complexity (VPC, SSO, custom routing).

[19:10] Rafael: any gotchas around rate limits and idempotency?
[19:16] Liam: typical gotchas: reusing idempotency keys incorrectly across different payloads; long-lived idempotency windows causing stale caching; and mistaken client retries that don't carry same conversation history. we recommend short idempotency TTLs and explicit conversation ids.

[20:00] (customer asks about error classification)
[20:07] Priya: we classify errors into transient, capacity, and model-safety. transient -> retry with backoff; capacity -> fallback to smaller model variant; safety -> reject and log for review. console has filters for these.

[22:00] Maya: do you provide sample SDKs? node, python?
[22:05] Ava: yes node, python, go, java-ish SDKs; they include streaming helpers and idempotency wrappers. we'll share code samples in the follow up.

[24:30] (brief silence)
[24:45] Ethan: for the sandbox run are there quotas? can we get a burst for a day to run load tests?
[24:54] Ava: we can temporarily raise sandbox quotas for a coordinated benchmark run, yes. we'll need the payloads and target qps.

[26:12] (demo: console cost view)
[26:25] Liam: cost per token view, attribution by key and route. you can pin a cost SLO and get alerts when projected monthly spend exceeds a threshold.
[26:48] Rafael: useful. do we get per-route latency SLOs in the hosted plan?
[26:55] Ava: hosted has best-effort latency commitments; dedicated has SLA-backed p95 guarantees. we'll include SLA options in the pricing sheet.

[28:00] Maya: i noticed earlier you mentioned 'resume offsets' — what is the typical resume window?
[28:06] Priya: typically 60-90 seconds TTL for resume state in hosted, configurable for dedicated/private. it's meant for network glitches, not long pauses.

[29:20] (customer probes about privacy — model training again)
[29:28] Ava: to reiterate — enterprise accounts can opt-out of training. we also offer a sandbox mode with telemetry disabled. will send formal policy doc.

[31:00] Liam: quick walkthrough of code pattern for streaming: open SSE, listen for 'delta' events, append to buffer, on 'done' event validate checksum. we also suggest local dedupe using message ids.
[31:35] Ethan: checksum? do you mean a sequence id?
[31:40] Liam: yes sequence ids plus final checksum if you want end-to-end verification.

[33:00] (transcript has small ASR hiccup: "redwood console" as "red wood console")

[34:10] Maya: ok high-level recap — you're recommending: 1) enable streaming with idempotency keys, 2) implement exponential backoff with jitter, 3) use small batch windows and KV caching for cost savings, 4) plan for a short resume TTL and use dedicated pools for strict SLOs. is that right?
[34:34] Ava: yup, exactly.

[35:00] Rafael: what's the onboarding support like? will we have an assigned solutions engineer?
[35:06] Ava: yes for committed pilots and reserved capacity we assign an SE and CSM. Priya and Liam would be on those calls.

[36:20] (customer asks for references)
[36:26] Ava: we can share anonymized references and a short benchmark sheet from a comparable media customer. i'll include that in the follow up.

[37:10] Ethan: ok last question: in failure modes, do you have automatic fallback to cheaper model variants when capacity cold?
[37:18] Priya: yes smart routing can fallback to compatible variants; you can configure per-route fallback policies. console shows which variants are compatible. note: sometimes model names are transcribed wrong in the notes (e.g., 'x-giant' vs 'x-giant-quant').

[38:40] (wrap-up)
[38:45] Ava: thanks all — recapping next steps. we'll: send pricing + SLA options, SOC2 kit and security whitepaper, provision sandbox with raised quota for benchmark, schedule security deep dive with Jenny and Rafael, and run the quantization evaluation on your prompt set.
[39:10] Maya: sounds good. can we get the sandbox creds by friday?
[39:15] Ava: yes we'll aim for friday.
[39:20] Rafael: thanks for the demo.
[39:23] Ethan: great session.
[39:28] (meeting ends)

Notes: transcript includes occasional ASR mis-labels and filler words. timestamps approximate every 15–90s depending on speaker turns.
